paper_metadata.title: Distantly supervised Web relation extraction for knowledge base population
paper_metadata.abstract: The paper proposes distantly supervised relation extraction from heterogeneous Web pages for knowledge-base population. It addresses data sparsity, noise, and lexical ambiguity through cross-domain entity recognition, cross-sentence extraction with unsupervised coreference methods, statistical training-seed selection, and integration of relation mentions from multiple Web sources.

paper_metadata-authors-01-01.excerpt: Isabelle Augenstein, Diana Maynard and Fabio Ciravegna

paper_metadata-abstract-05-01.excerpt: Our approach reduces the impact of data sparsity by making entity recognition tools more robust across domains and extracting relations across sentence boundaries using unsupervised co-reference resolution methods.

paper_metadata-abstract-05-02.excerpt: To combine information extracted from multiple sources for populating knowledge bases we present and evaluate several information integration strategies.

problem_addressed-06-01.excerpt: Extracting information from Web pages for populating large, cross-domain knowledge bases requires methods which are suitable across domains, do not require manual effort to adapt to new domains, are able to deal with noise, and integrate information extracted from different Web pages.

problem_addressed: Populate large cross-domain knowledge bases from unstructured heterogeneous Web text without manual domain adaptation. The authors target shortcomings of prior distant supervision for Web extraction: unrecognised nonstandard entities, sentence-boundary restrictions that cause sparsity, ambiguous object lexicalisations that create noisy labels, and lack of integration across redundant Web documents.

methodology.description: Execution pipeline: (1) select seven Freebase classes and five to seven properties each; retrieve entities and Web pages with Google Search queries; (2) extract HTML text with Jsoup, then use Stanford CoreNLP for sentence splitting, tokenisation, POS tagging, time normalisation, NER, and optionally coreference; (3) add a custom boundary-only entity recogniser using noun/capitalised-word sequences and quoted strings; (4) align subject/object lexicalisations from Freebase to automatically label positive and negative sentence candidates; (5) filter ambiguous training seeds with Stop, Unam, Stat, and StatRes; (6) extract lexical, POS, context, order, and NE features; (7) train one multiclass logistic-regression classifier per class to predict a property or NONE for each relation mention; (8) support a relaxed paragraph setting with Stanford or gazetteer-based coreference; and (9) aggregate mention predictions using Comb, Aggr, Limit, and MultiLab strategies to produce KB relations.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: The Freebase knowledge base supplies the schema-constrained classes, properties, subject/object entities, and their lexicalisations. Only triples already in Freebase are used for distant labels; extraction is performed per selected class and predicts its applicable properties.

input_output.input_type: Unstructured text extracted from HTML Web pages, retrieved by Google Search API and annotated using Freebase entity lexicalisations.
input_output.input_granularity: Web documents are split into paragraphs and sentences; normal extraction uses sentences containing a subject and another entity, while the relaxed setting considers paragraphs whose sentences can contain coreferent subject mentions.
input_output.output_representation: Schema-defined binary Freebase relation tuples/facts: a subject, predicate/property, and object; relation-mention predictions are aggregated into relations for knowledge-base population.

models_and_tools: Multiclass logistic regression; one classifier per Freebase class and model
Stanford CoreNLP for sentence splitting, tokenisation, POS tagging, time normalisation, 7-class NER, and CorefS
Custom boundary-only NER based on noun/capitalised-word sequences and quoted strings
Google Search API for corpus retrieval
Freebase API for selected entity/property retrieval
WordNet and Wikipedia redirection pages for class synonym/hypernym/hyponym gazetteers
Bergsma and Lin Web co-occurrence gender/number gazetteers for CorefN/CorefP
datasets: Author-constructed Web corpus of approximately one million pages from 76,000 websites

Freebase-derived hold-out relation dataset covering seven selected classes: Musical Artist, Politician, Business Operation, Educational Institution, Film, Book, and River; five to seven prominent properties per class
For corpus construction, 1,800–2,200 entities per class with values for all selected properties; up to ten Web pages per entity

baselines: Reimplemented Mintz et al. lexical-feature distant-supervision model: Stanford NERC only, 1% unrelated entities as negative training data, tuple-level feature aggregation
Authors' Baseline: Stanford NERC plus custom NER, all negative training data, no seed filtering
Comb information-integration model for comparison with Aggr, Limit, and MultiLab variants
CorefS Stanford CoreNLP coreference model for comparison with gazetteer-based CorefN and CorefP
evaluation.setting: Automatic hold-out evaluation for knowledge-base population: relation tuples from the selected Freebase portion are split 50%/50% for training/testing after the Web corpus is automatically annotated with known Freebase relations. Results are micro-averaged over relations/classes; recall is bounded by an estimated top line because not every KB tuple is textually represented in the retrieved corpus. The authors state that direct comparison to Mintz et al. is not possible because that work used Wikipedia and a different evaluation setup.

value: Across all relations, the best reported relaxed model—CorefN with Stop+Unam+Stat75 seed selection and MultiLab+Limit75 integration—achieved micro precision 0.857 and recall 0.0289; its estimated recall top line was 0.0917.

For seed selection under MultiLab+Limit75, the authors' Baseline reached P=0.770, R=0.0401; Stop+Unam+Stat75 raised precision to 0.801 while lowering recall to 0.0243. Excessive filtering (Stat25) reduced precision to 0.767 and recall to 0.00128.
For integration using CorefN+Stop+Unam+Stat75, Comb achieved P=0.742/R=0.0328, Aggr P=0.813/R=0.0341, MultiLab P=0.837/R=0.0307, and MultiLab+Limit75 P=0.857/R=0.0289.

The best extended (CorefN) model improved precision and recall over the best normal model for Musical Artist, Politician, River, Business Operation, and Book; e.g., River changed from P=0.875/R=0.0234 to P=0.889/R=0.0902, while Educational Institution and Film did not improve precision.
The authors conclude that cross-sentence extraction increased recall by up to 25% depending on model and precision by 8% on average; statistical seed selection increased precision by 3% on average.

value: The system is designed for heterogeneous Web pages rather than a single narrow domain, combining a news-trained NERC with a custom recogniser for nonstandard entity types such as tracks and albums.

It handles relation evidence across sentence boundaries using both standard and lightweight gazetteer-based coreference alternatives; the latter achieved performance comparable to Stanford CoreNLP coreference on this Web corpus.
It treats redundant relation mentions as evidence to integrate for KB population and permits mutually compatible multiple labels through MultiLab.

[Review-level inference] The design is modular and ablation-oriented: seed filtering, coreference strategy, and aggregation strategy are separately varied, which makes the source of performance trade-offs inspectable within this experimental setting.

value: The custom NER identifies boundaries but does not classify named entities, leaving the NE-class feature unavailable for candidates found only by that recogniser.

Entity-boundary and subject-identification errors are the two largest error groups. Non-greedy matching can train on a partial noun phrase rather than the correct complete phrase, and the model can attribute an object relation to the wrong subject.
Seed filtering trades recall for precision; removing too many positive training instances can damage both.

[Review-level inference] The reported recall values are low and the estimated top line is itself low, so the approach's KB-population coverage is constrained by what the retrieval and candidate-identification pipeline surfaces, even when precision is high.

[Review-level inference] The automatic Freebase hold-out measures recovery of known KB tuples in a corpus labelled from that KB; it does not establish correctness or novelty of facts beyond the reference KB.

The method may not suit scenarios with only a small document corpus or very few relation tuples in the training KB, because distant supervision requires either a very large corpus or a large KB.
The estimated recall top line is not exact because the corpus is too large to manually examine every sentence.
The system does not account for an entity appearing in more than one relation, which can create incorrect positive context weights and wrong-subject predictions.
